abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify regions of the genome linked to disease, but they do not tell us which cells are involved. Researchers often address that question by testing marker genes from single-cell atlases. We asked how much the answer changes when those markers are defined differently. Reconstructing a published endometriosis analysis, we found that selecting genes with large fold changes in either direction prioritized venous endothelium, whereas selecting up-regulated genes prioritized decidual stroma (the latter was not significant after within-family false-discovery correction). A calibrated benchmark, six-trait control panel, and donor-level checks showed why neither rule can be trusted on its own. In an independent RNA atlas, stromal programs were repeatedly prioritized, although closely related perivascular states remained plausible. We then examined an independent molecular layer: chromatin accessibility in 36,073 nuclei from 12 endometrial biopsies. The initially specified analysis found enrichment of endometriosis heritability in stromal accessible chromatin (z = 4.11, one-sided p = 2 x 10^-5). In a later, more stringent joint model with baselineLD v2.2, the stromal coefficient remained positive (z = 3.83, p = 6.47 x 10^-5) and exceeded the epithelial coefficient (z = 3.68, p = 1.18 x 10^-4). Both effects remained nominally significant when each biopsy was excluded in turn (12/12 analyses). The association was also seen for leiomyoma, and the endometriosis GWAS share participants. Together, these findings support a broad stromal regulatory context for part of inherited endometriosis risk, but do not establish a unique causal cell state or a lesion cell of origin.
